title: Contribution of Microscopy to a Better Understanding of the Nano Anatomy of Parasitic Protists
content: Parasitic protists comprise many species, including some that are pathogenic for humans and animals of economic interest. They are unicellular organisms containing most of the characteristic organelles found in mammalian cells. However, they also present specialized organelles and cytoskeletal structures that maintain the intracellular architecture and participate in dynamic changes that occur during the cell differentiation. They have been analyzed by our group using several microscopy techniques. T. cruzi has a complex life cycle involving three developmental stages. Tritrichomonas foetus is maintained in axenic cultures as flagellated trophozoites that under stress conditions can internalize the flagella forming rounded forms known as pseudocysts. The epimastigote form of T. cruzi presents a single flagellum that emerges from the flagellar pocket located at the anterior region of the protozoan. The initial portion of the flagellum attaches to the protozoan surface and then ends freely. At the basis of the flagellum there is a dense structure localized within the unique and highly ramified mitochondrion, known as the kinetoplast. It is formed due to a condensation of thousands of DNA minicircles and a few maxicircles that account for about 30% of the total cell DNA, There is one single nucleus and the cytoplasm contains many ribosomes, lipid droplets, endoplasmic reticulum, sub-pellicular microtubules, and special organelles such as the glycosomes, acidocalcisomes and reservosomes. Tritrichomonas foetus is characterized by the presence of three anterior flagella and one recurrent flagellum. It presents a complex cytoskeleton where structures such as the costa, parabasal filaments, and axoxtyle (composed of microtubules) are seen. The cytoplasm contains hydrogenosomes, glycogen particles and a well-developed Golgi complex.
